pos: n. (the Clarendon Code, 1661–1665, the four penal statutes against English Nonconformity)
etymology: Clarendon, the title of Edward Hyde, Charles II's chancellor; Latin codex, a book of statutes.
biblical_def: The Clarendon Code is the collective name for four statutes passed by the Cavalier Parliament after the Restoration, aimed at breaking Puritan Nonconformity in England. The Corporation Act of 1661 excluded from municipal office any man who would not receive the sacrament in the parish church; the Act of Uniformity of 1662 required every minister to declare unfeigned assent to the whole Book of Common Prayer; the Conventicle Act of 1664 made it criminal for more than four persons to meet for worship outside the establishment; the Five Mile Act of 1665 forbade an ejected minister to come within five miles of his old parish or any corporate town. They were named for Lord Chancellor Clarendon, though he did not design them all, and they were enforced with varying severity for a quarter of a century. Their effect was to create English Dissent as a permanent body: some two thousand ministers were silenced, thousands of people were fined or imprisoned, and Bunyan wrote in Bedford gaol. “Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?” (Psa 94:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a code as a collection of the laws of a nation, and penal as enacting punishment.
webster_full: CODE, n. A collection or digest of laws; a book of the civil law.
PE'NAL, a. Enacting punishment; denouncing the punishment of offenses.
CONFORM'ITY, n. Correspondence with a model or example; compliance.
scriptures: Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
Act 4:18
And they called them, and commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus.
Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
corruption_summary: The four Restoration statutes that made English Dissent a permanent body.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Code is worth studying for its method, which is not peculiar to the seventeenth century. It did not forbid the Puritan faith. It attached civil penalties to acting on it: no office without the parish sacrament, no ministry without assent to a book, no meeting above four, no residence near one's own people. Conscience was left formally free and made practically ruinous.

The principle to recover is that such laws are to be recognised for what they are. The psalm names a throne that “frameth mischief by a law” (Psa 94:20), and the council at Jerusalem “commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus” (Act 4:18) with every appearance of legality. Peter's reply remains the only one available (Act 4:19).
roots_summary: Hebrew choq (H2706), a statute; amal (H5999), mischief, trouble; Greek diogmos (G1375), persecution.
roots_lines: Hebrew choq (H2706) — a statute, decree, ordinance; Psalm 94:20.
Hebrew yatsar (H3335) — to form, frame, fashion; Psalm 94:20.

“commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus” (Act 4:18) — the Conventicle Act in substance.
“all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12) — two thousand ministers.

pos: n. (the Act of Uniformity, 1662, which required assent to the Book of Common Prayer and ejected two thousand ministers)
etymology: Latin uniformis, of one form; Latin actum, a thing done, a statute.
biblical_def: The Act of Uniformity of 1662 required every minister, schoolmaster and tutor in England to declare before St Bartholomew's Day his unfeigned assent and consent to all and everything contained in and prescribed by the revised Book of Common Prayer; to renounce the Solemn League and Covenant; to abjure the taking up of arms against the king on any pretence; and, if not episcopally ordained, to be reordained. The Prayer Book itself was not published until weeks before the deadline, so that many were required to assent to a book they had not read. Between eighteen hundred and two thousand ministers refused and lost their livings, among them Richard Baxter, Thomas Manton, Joseph Caryl, Philip Henry and John Howe — the Great Ejection. The Nonconformists' objection was never to a liturgy as such but to the terms: unfeigned assent to every word of a human composition, on pain of losing a divine calling. “But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9) was the text most often cited against it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines uniformity as conformity to one rule or mode, and assent as the act of agreeing to anything.
webster_full: UNIFORM'ITY, n. Conformity to one rule or mode; resemblance to itself; consistency.
ASSENT', n. The act of agreeing to anything; consent; agreement to a proposal.
LIT'URGY, n. A formulary of public devotions; a prescribed form of prayer.
scriptures: Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Gal 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
corruption_summary: The 1662 statute requiring unfeigned assent to every word of the Prayer Book.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Act is widely treated as a quarrel over ceremonies, surplices and the sign of the cross, as though two thousand men gave up house and bread over vestments. The sticking point was the word unfeigned. A minister had to swear inward agreement with everything in a book, which no honest reader of any long human document can do.

The principle to recover is that the conscience is bound to God and may not be pledged to a man's composition as though it were Scripture. “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9) describes the fault precisely, and Paul's test applies to every subscription: “if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ” (Gal 1:10).
roots_summary: Greek entalma (G1778), a commandment of men; paradosis (G3862), tradition; areskos from aresko (G700), to please.
roots_lines: Greek entalma (G1778) — an injunction, commandment of men; Matthew 15:9.

“after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world” (Col 2:8) — the Nonconformist case.
“if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ” (Gal 1:10) — St Bartholomew's Day, 1662.

pos: n. (the Five Mile Act, 1665, which barred ejected ministers from their old parishes and from corporate towns)
etymology: Old English fif, five, and mil, from Latin mille passus, a thousand paces.
biblical_def: The Five Mile Act of 1665, properly the Nonconformists Act, forbade any minister ejected under the Act of Uniformity to come within five miles of any parish from which he had been removed, or of any city or corporate town, unless he swore the Oxford oath — that he would never at any time endeavour any alteration of government in church or state. It also barred such men from keeping school. The penalty was forty pounds, a crushing sum for a man without a living. It was passed at Oxford, where Parliament had fled from the Great Plague, and its design was plain: to cut the silenced pastor off from the people who still looked to him and from the towns where he might find work or charity. Many obeyed the letter and lived in villages, preaching in houses by night; some, like Thomas Vincent and Thomas Doolittle, went back into plague-stricken London when the conforming clergy fled, and preached in empty pulpits to the dying. “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to banish as to compel to leave one's country, and an oath as a solemn affirmation with an appeal to God.
webster_full: BAN'ISH, v.t. To compel a person to leave his own country; to drive away.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God.
SO'JOURN, v.i. To dwell for a time; to dwell or live in a place as a temporary resident.
scriptures: For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another: for verily I say unto you, Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Psa 56:8
Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?
corruption_summary: The 1665 statute that drove silenced ministers five miles from their own people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Act is a textbook case of a persecution designed to look reasonable. No one was burned and no doctrine was forbidden; a man was simply required either to swear he would never seek any change in church or state, or to live five miles from everyone he knew and keep no school.

The principle to recover is that a pilgrim people are not undone by displacement: “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). Our Lord anticipated the arrangement — “when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another” (Mat 10:23) — and the wanderings are counted: “Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle” (Psa 56:8).
roots_summary: Greek meno (G3306), to continue, abide; pheugo (G5343), to flee; Hebrew nod (H5112), wandering.
roots_lines: Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, continue, remain; Hebrews 13:14.
Greek epizeteo (G1934) — to seek after, search for; Hebrews 13:14.
usage: “here have we no continuing city” (Heb 13:14) — five miles from home.
“when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another” (Mat 10:23) — the ejected ministers' practice.
“Thou tellest my wanderings” (Psa 56:8) — the Oxford oath refused.

pos: n. (the Conventicle Acts, 1664 and 1670, which made Nonconformist worship a criminal offence)
etymology: Latin conventiculum, a small assembly, diminutive of conventus, a gathering.
biblical_def: The Conventicle Act of 1664 made it an offence for more than four persons, besides the household, to assemble for religious worship otherwise than according to the liturgy of the Church of England. The penalties rose by stages to transportation for a third conviction. It lapsed in 1668 and was replaced in 1670 by a second and shrewder Act which lowered the fines but paid informers a share of them, laid heavy penalties on the preacher and on the owner of the house, and empowered a single magistrate to convict without a jury. That second Act turned persecution into a trade and produced the worst of the suffering: meetings were broken up by troopers, goods were seized, and prisons at Newgate, Aylesbury and Bedford filled. John Bunyan had already been taken in 1660 for preaching at Lower Samsell and spent twelve years in Bedford gaol, writing. The Dissenters went on meeting in woods, barns and upper rooms, and defended themselves from the plain command: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a conventicle as an assembly for worship, used of a meeting of dissenters; and an informer as one who gives intelligence against another.
webster_full: CONVEN'TICLE, n. An assembly or meeting; a meeting for religious worship, applied to dissenters.
INFORM'ER, n. One who gives information of a breach of law to a magistrate.
ASSEM'BLING, ppr. Coming or bringing together in one place.
scriptures: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
And when he had considered the thing, he came to the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark; where many were gathered together praying.
Mal 3:16

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.
Psa 42:4
When I remember these things, I pour out my soul in me: for I had gone with the multitude, I went with them to the house of God, with the voice of joy and praise, with a multitude that kept holyday.
corruption_summary: The 1664 and 1670 Acts that criminalised Dissenting worship and paid informers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The second Conventicle Act did something worth remembering: it made persecution profitable. Informers were paid a third of the fines, so the enforcement no longer depended on the zeal of magistrates but on the appetite of neighbours. That is a far more effective instrument than an occasional martyrdom.

The principle to recover is that assembling is commanded and therefore not negotiable (Heb 10:25). When the public place was shut, the church met in a house, as it had at the beginning: “he came to the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark; where many were gathered together praying” (Act 12:12). The persecuted habit of mutual speech is itself noticed in heaven (Mal 3:16).
roots_summary: Greek episunagoge (G1997), an assembling together; egkataleipo (G1459), to forsake; sunathroizo (G4867), to gather together.
roots_lines: Greek episunagoge (G1997) — a gathering together, assembly; Hebrews 10:25.
Greek sunathroizo (G4867) — to assemble, gather together; Acts 12:12.
Hebrew chagag (H2287) — to keep a feast, hold holyday; Psalm 42:4.
usage: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) — the Dissenters' answer.
“where many were gathered together praying” (Act 12:12) — worship in houses.
“they that feared the LORD spake often one to another” (Mal 3:16) — under the informers.

pos: n. (the Toleration Act, 1689, which gave English Dissenters freedom of worship under licence)
biblical_def: The Toleration Act of 1689, passed in the first year of William and Mary, granted to Protestant Dissenters who would take the oaths of allegiance and subscribe thirty-four of the Thirty-nine Articles the freedom to worship in licensed meeting-houses with unlocked doors, and exempted their ministers from the penalties of the Clarendon Code. It was a limited measure and was never called a grant of liberty by its framers: Roman Catholics and antitrinitarians were excluded, the Test and Corporation Acts still barred Dissenters from office and from the universities, and tithes to the parish church were still due. But it ended a quarter-century of criminal prosecution for worship, and within a few years hundreds of meeting-houses were licensed and built. The generation that had been fined, gaoled and driven five miles from home received it with a gratitude later ages have found excessive. They had prayed for exactly this: “that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2), and they knew who had turned the king's heart (Pro 21:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines toleration as the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, and a licence as authority given to do some act.
webster_full: TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state; freedom from penalty.
LI'CENSE, n. Authority or liberty given to do or forbear any act.
DISSENT'ER, n. One who separates from the service and worship of the established church.
scriptures: For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.
Pro 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
Mic 4:4
But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid: for the mouth of the LORD of hosts hath spoken it.
Act 9:31
Then had the churches rest throughout all Judaea and Galilee and Samaria, and were edified; and walking in the fear of the Lord, and in the comfort of the Holy Ghost, were multiplied.
corruption_summary: The 1689 Act that ended criminal prosecution of Dissenting worship in England.
corruption_paragraphs: Toleration has since become a word for the proposition that all religious claims are equally valid, and so a church is now expected to purchase its liberty by professing that its own doctrine is one opinion among many. The Act of 1689 did nothing of the kind. It required subscription to thirty-four Articles and excluded those who denied the Trinity; it tolerated worship, not indifference.

The principle to recover is what such liberty is for: “that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2). The rest that the early churches had was spent being edified and multiplied (Act 9:31), and the picture Micah gives — “they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid” (Mic 4:4) — is a mercy to be used, not a verdict on truth.
roots_summary: Greek hesuchios (G2272), quiet; eusebeia (G2150), godliness; Hebrew charad (H2729), to make afraid.
roots_lines: Hebrew charad (H2729) — to tremble, make afraid; Micah 4:4.
Hebrew nata (H5186) — to stretch out, turn; Proverbs 21:1.
usage: “that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2) — what 1689 granted.
“The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD” (Pro 21:1) — how the Dissenters read it.
“Then had the churches rest” (Act 9:31) — the licensed meeting-houses.

pos: n. (the Declarations of Indulgence, 1662, 1672 and 1687–88, royal suspensions of the penal laws)
etymology: Latin declarare, to make clear; indulgentia, a granting of favour, remission.
biblical_def: The Declarations of Indulgence were attempts by Charles II and James II to suspend the penal laws against Nonconformists and Roman Catholics by royal prerogative rather than by Act of Parliament. Charles issued one in 1662, withdrew it, and issued a second in 1672 which licensed over fifteen hundred Dissenting preachers before Parliament forced its cancellation in 1673. James II issued declarations in 1687 and 1688 and ordered the second read from every pulpit, which produced the trial of the Seven Bishops. The Dissenters were deeply divided over them. The relief was real and immediate — Bunyan was licensed in 1672 — but the instrument was a claim that the king could set aside a statute at will, and a liberty granted that way could be revoked the same way, as 1673 proved. Most of the leading Nonconformists refused James's indulgence, judging the price too high and the motive transparent. Their reasoning was not merely political: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines indulgence as favour granted, and prerogative as an exclusive or peculiar privilege.
webster_full: INDUL'GENCE, n. Favor granted; liberality; gratification; remission of the penalty.
PREROG'ATIVE, n. An exclusive or peculiar privilege; a right or power belonging to an office.
SUSPEND', v.t. To cause to cease for a time; to intermit; to stay.
scriptures: Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
Jer 17:5
Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.
Isa 2:22
Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils: for wherein is he to be accounted of?
Pro 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
corruption_summary: Royal suspensions of the penal laws, which the Dissenters mostly refused to buy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Indulgences pose a question churches still face: whether to accept relief from an authority acting outside its own law, when the relief is genuine and urgently needed. Fifteen hundred licences in 1672 meant preaching, and the cancellation of 1673 meant prison again. The men who refused in 1687 were not ungrateful; they had learned what a prerogative gift is worth.

The principle to recover is where a church's confidence rests. “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm” (Jer 17:5) is not a counsel of political withdrawal, since the king's heart is still in the LORD's hand (Pro 21:1); it is a warning against making a patron's favour the ground of the church's standing.
roots_summary: Hebrew nadib (H5081), a prince, noble; batach (H982), to trust; neshamah (H5397), breath.
roots_lines: Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, be confident; Psalm 146:3.
usage: “Put not your trust in princes” (Psa 146:3) — why most refused James's indulgence.
“Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm” (Jer 17:5) — a prerogative liberty.
“Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils” (Isa 2:22) — 1672 and then 1673.

pos: n. (the Savoy Conference, 1661, the last negotiation between Anglicans and Presbyterians over the Prayer Book)
etymology: Savoy, the London palace where the conference met; Latin conferre, to bring together.
biblical_def: The Savoy Conference met from April to July 1661 at the Bishop of London's lodging in the Savoy, twelve bishops and twelve Presbyterian divines with nine assistants each, commissioned by Charles II to review the Book of Common Prayer and consider the Nonconformists' objections. Richard Baxter was the Presbyterians' chief spokesman and drew up an alternative liturgy, the Reformed Liturgy, in a fortnight. The Presbyterians asked for small and specific things: that kneeling at communion, the surplice, the sign of the cross in baptism and godparents be made optional rather than required, that unfit persons not be admitted to the table, and that ministers be free to pray in their own words. The bishops, secure in the new Parliament, conceded almost nothing; of some six hundred requests, about seventeen trivial alterations were made. The conference broke up having settled nothing, and the Act of Uniformity followed within a year. “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated” (Jam 3:17) was not much in evidence on either side of the table.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a conference as a meeting for consultation, and a concession as the act of yielding or granting something demanded.
webster_full: CON'FERENCE, n. A meeting of two or more persons for consulting on an important subject.
CONCES'SION, n. The act of granting or yielding; the thing yielded.
RU'BRIC, n. Directions printed in books of law and in prayer books; so termed because written in red.
scriptures: Jam 3:17
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
corruption_summary: The 1661 conference that conceded almost nothing and made 1662 inevitable.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Savoy is a lesson in the difference between a negotiation and a formality. Both parties were commissioned to confer; one of them had the votes and knew it, and so the conference became a record of positions rather than a search for terms. Baxter's mistake, which he later admitted, was to answer a closed door with a longer paper.

The principle to recover is that heavenly wisdom is “easy to be intreated” (Jam 3:17) — a quality that costs the stronger party something and is therefore the test of whether a conference is real. “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger” (Pro 15:1), and six hundred requests met with seventeen trifles is a grievous answer however softly phrased.
roots_summary: Greek sophia (G4678), wisdom; eupeithes (G2138), easy to be intreated; epieikes (G1933), gentle.
roots_lines: Greek eupeithes (G2138) — compliant, easy to be intreated; James 3:17.
usage: “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated” (Jam 3:17) — what the Savoy lacked.
“A soft answer turneth away wrath” (Pro 15:1) — seventeen alterations out of six hundred.
“the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6) — the pattern it failed to follow.

pos: n. (the Happy Union, 1691–1695, the short-lived agreement of London Presbyterians and Congregationalists)
etymology: Middle English hap, chance, fortune, whence happy; Latin unio, oneness.
biblical_def: The Happy Union was the agreement of 1691 by which the Presbyterian and Congregational ministers in and about London formed a single body under Heads of Agreement, pooling their funds, their lecture, and their examination of candidates. The old quarrel of the 1640s over church government had been worn down by thirty years of shared suffering under the Clarendon Code, and with toleration granted in 1689 both sides thought the breach could be closed. It lasted four years. The trouble came not over polity but over doctrine: Richard Davis of Rothwell was accused of antinomian preaching, and in the controversy that followed the republication of Tobias Crisp's sermons divided the union into parties, the Presbyterians suspecting antinomianism and the Congregationalists suspecting neonomianism. By 1695 the common fund was split and the union was over, though the Heads of Agreement remained in print as a standing proposal. “Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another” (Rom 14:19) — it proved easier to subscribe than to practise.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines union as the junction of two or more things, concord; and agreement as harmony of opinion or sentiment.
webster_full: U'NION, n. The act of joining two or more things into one; concord; agreement.
AGREE'MENT, n. Harmony of opinion, action or character; a compact or bargain.
FUND, n. A stock or capital; money set apart for a specific purpose.
scriptures: Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another.
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Jam 3:18
And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace.
corruption_summary: The 1691 London union of Presbyterians and Congregationalists, broken in four years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Happy Union is instructive precisely because it failed over the thing nobody expected. Both sides had braced for a fight about elders and synods, the issue that had divided them for fifty years; what broke them was the gospel itself — how free the offer is, and what place the law has in a believer's standing.

The principle to recover is that peace is something followed after, with an aim: “things wherewith one may edify another” (Rom 14:19). A union whose only shared ground is a shared grievance will not survive the first doctrinal question, and the fruit of righteousness “is sown in peace of them that make peace” (Jam 3:18) — sown, that is, by patient work and not by a signature.
roots_lines: Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, follow after; Romans 14:19.
Greek katartizo (G2675) — to join together, perfect; 1 Corinthians 1:10.
usage: “follow after the things which make for peace” (Rom 14:19) — the Heads of Agreement, 1691.
“that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — what four years could not secure.
“the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace” (Jam 3:18) — and it takes longer than a signature.

pos: n. (the Salters' Hall synod, 1719, the London Dissenting assembly that refused to require subscription on the Trinity)
etymology: Salters' Hall, the London livery-company hall where the ministers met.
biblical_def: Salters' Hall was the meeting of some hundred and fifty London Dissenting ministers in February and March 1719, called to advise on a dispute at Exeter where two ministers were suspected of Arianism. The advice sought was practical; the question that split the assembly was whether their letter should include a declaration of belief in the Trinity in the words of the first of the Thirty-nine Articles or the Westminster Catechism. By fifty-seven votes to fifty-three the assembly decided that no such subscription should be required, on the stated ground that Scripture alone is the rule and no human form may be imposed. The minority withdrew, and English Dissent divided into subscribers and non-subscribers. The practical consequence is a matter of record: within two generations most of the English Presbyterian congregations whose ministers took the non-subscribing side had become Arian and then Unitarian, while the Independents and Particular Baptists, who subscribed, remained orthodox. “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) turned out to be a practical instruction and not a formality.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subscription as the act of signing in attestation, and nonsubscriber as one who does not subscribe or assent.
webster_full: SUBSCRIP'TION, n. The act of subscribing or writing one's name underneath; attestation.
NONSUBSCRI'BER, n. One who does not subscribe or assent to something.
A'RIANISM, n. The doctrines of the Arians, who denied the divinity of Christ.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Joh 5:23
That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him.
Heb 1:8
But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom.
corruption_summary: The 1719 vote that refused to require a Trinitarian subscription, and what followed.
corruption_paragraphs: The non-subscribers' argument was not a denial of the Trinity. Most of them believed it; they held that requiring a creed in human words sets a form above Scripture, and that an honest man should be asked only whether he believes the Bible. It is exactly the argument that would be made in Ulster a few years later, and in Scotland, and in America, and it is still made.

The principle to recover is that the argument has been tested and the results are in. A church with nothing to subscribe cannot examine a candidate, cannot try a charge, and cannot tell its own people what it holds. The apostolic instruction is to hold fast a form of sound words (2Ti 1:13) and to contend for the faith once delivered (Jude 1:3) — and the honour of the Son is not a detail (Joh 5:23).
roots_summary: Greek hupotuposis (G5296), a pattern, outline; homologia (G3671), confession; timao (G5091), to honour.
roots_lines: Greek hupotuposis (G5296) — an outline, form, pattern; 2 Timothy 1:13.
usage: “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — the motion that lost by four votes.
“earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jude 1:3) — the minority's case.
“He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father” (Joh 5:23) — what the next generation lost.

pos: n. (Philip Henry, 1631–1696, ejected minister of Worthenbury, father of Matthew Henry)
etymology: Greek Philippos, lover of horses; Old German Heimerich, ruler of the home.
biblical_def: Philip Henry was born in Whitehall, where his father was keeper of the orchard, educated at Westminster under Busby and at Christ Church, and settled at Worthenbury in Flintshire. He was ejected in 1662 under the Act of Uniformity and spent the remaining thirty-four years at Broad Oak, a silenced minister who preached in his own house, catechised his children and his neighbours' children, and kept a diary that is one of the plainest records of Nonconformist family religion. He was twice prosecuted under the Five Mile Act and once imprisoned. He is best known now as the father of Matthew Henry, whose commentary came out of the household worship Philip conducted twice a day for three decades; and his sayings have outlived his sermons — that he would rather beg his bread than sin against conscience, and that family religion is the strength of the church. “but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15) was the text of the home he ran. He died at Broad Oak in 1696, having lived to see toleration granted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a household as those who dwell under the same roof, and catechise as to instruct by asking questions.
webster_full: HOUSE'HOLD, n. Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family.
CAT'ECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions and correcting the answers.
DI'ARY, n. A register of daily events or transactions; a journal.
scriptures: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way. O when wilt thou come unto me? I will walk within my house with a perfect heart.
Act 10:2
A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
corruption_summary: The ejected minister of Worthenbury whose household worship produced Matthew Henry.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Philip Henry does stand against the assumption that a silenced ministry is a wasted one. He lost his pulpit at thirty-one and never had another. What he had instead was a house, a diary, and two services a day for thirty-four years, and out of it came the commentary that has been read in more homes than any sermon he could have preached at Worthenbury.

The principle to recover is that a father's charge over his own house is a ministry and not a consolation prize: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15), and “I will walk within my house with a perfect heart” (Psa 101:2). Cornelius is commended as “one that feared God with all his house” (Act 10:2) before he had heard the gospel preached at all.
